output.answer: As of November 11, 2026, the most recent proposed class action was Habel v. Synchrony Bank (filed June 1, 2026), alleging prerecorded debt-collection calls after consent was revoked; the case was dismissed with prejudice on September 10, 2026 after a settlement notice, without class certification. Other significant cases include S.G. v. Synchrony Bank (2024), alleging that CareCredit interest rates exceeded New York’s usury cap; Taylor v. Synchrony Bank (2024), alleging an SCRA-related “veteran penalty” that raised rates for servicemembers after active duty; and the certified Lucas TCPA class action, which settled for $2.6 million over prerecorded calls about accounts that did not belong to recipients. Earlier matters included Dermer (2020, alleged mishandling of PayPal Credit promotional purchases), Mott (2018, alleged autodialed collection calls), McMullen (2014, One World Fitness financing claims), and the separate Synchrony Financial securities class action, which settled for $34 million in 2023.
caveats: These are documented proposed or certified class actions located in the reviewed sources, not a claim that every complaint ever naming Synchrony has been identified.
The allegations in the complaints are plaintiffs’ allegations; they are not findings that Synchrony Bank violated the law.
The securities case was against Synchrony Financial and executives rather than solely Synchrony Bank, but it concerns the Synchrony enterprise and is included separately for clarity.
The sources reviewed do not establish a final merits ruling or class certification for S.G. or Taylor.

output.question: What class action lawsuits has Synchrony Bank faced?

key_facts.fact: Habel v. Synchrony Bank was filed June 1, 2026; the docket describes a TCPA case and records dismissal with prejudice on September 10, 2026 after a notice of settlement.
The Habel complaint alleged prerecorded debt-collection calls after the plaintiff revoked consent.
S.G. v. Synchrony Bank was filed August 19, 2024 and alleged that CareCredit rates of 32.99% and higher violated New York usury and consumer-protection law.
Taylor v. Synchrony Bank et al. alleged that Synchrony reclaimed servicemember benefits by raising rates and fees after active duty, violating the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act and related duties.

Lucas v. Synchrony Bank was conditionally certified as a class action and preliminarily approved for settlement on November 18, 2022; the settlement website states the fund was $2.6 million for specified prerecorded calls made from October 16, 2020 through November 18, 2022.
Dermer alleged that PayPal Credit and Synchrony Bank misrepresented promotional-purchase terms and failed to properly credit a return.
Mott alleged that Synchrony used an automated telephone dialing system to make unsolicited collection calls concerning a debt the plaintiff said she did not owe.
McMullen involved proposed class-action claims by One World Fitness customers who obtained financing from bank defendants including Synchrony.
The Synchrony Financial securities class action alleged misleading statements about underwriting and settled for $34 million; final approval was entered August 4, 2023.
